newsitem.title: UK: Vitamin lack may contribute to arthritis - study.
newsitem.headline: Vitamin lack may contribute to arthritis - study.

text.p: U.S. researchers said on Wednesday they may have found yet another reason for people to eat their vegetables -- vitamins such as A and E may protect against diseases like rheumatoid arthritis and lupus.
Tests on blood donations made by people who later developed rheumatoid arthritis and lupus showed low levels of vitamins A and E.
Dr George Comstock and colleagues at the Training Centre for Public Health in Hagerstown, Maryland looked at blood samples donated to a serum bank.
They traced people who later developed rheumatoid arthritis or lupus and compared the levels of vitamins in their blood to that of healthy donors.
Those who went on to get either disease -- both believed to be caused by the immune system mistakenly turning on itself -- had lower levels of vitamins A and E than those who did not.

Arthritis sufferers had especially low levels of beta carotene, which is found in fruits and vegetables and which the body converts to vitamin A, they wrote in a report in the British Medical Association's Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases.
They said the vitamins, known to protect against charged particles known as free radicals, could defend the joints against damage done by the free radicals.
Lupus affects up to one or two percent of the populaton, and nine out of 10 sufferers are female.
Rheumatoid arthritis is much more common, affecting one in 20 in Britain. Both diseases cause pain, inflammation and other symptoms.
